newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Banker's notes accuse Austrian elite of wrongdoing.
newsitem.headline: Banker's notes accuse Austrian elite of wrongdoing.

text.p: Austrian far-right leader Joerg Haider said on Tuesday the suicide of a top banker was linked to an alleged tax evasion scandal involving senior figures in the country's banking and political establishment.
Gerhard Praschak, a board member of clearing house Kontrollbank (OeKB), shot himself in the head on Saturday.
Before killing himself, Praschak sent a 120-page document to opposition parties, including Haider's Freedom Party, a weekly news magazine and state prosecutors.

Haider said the documents described how Austria's two top banks had prompted OeKB's board in 1994 to secretly award its shareholders a special payment totalling 140 million schillings ($12 million) on which no tax was paid.
"Profits were drawn off and tax obligations not fulfilled," Haider told a news conference. "According to Praschak that was the wish of (Guido) Schmidt(-Chiari) and (Gerhard) Randa."
Randa, chief executive of partly state-controlled Bank Austria, heads OeKB's supervisory board.
Schmidt-Chiari, who until Tuesday was the chief executive of Creditanstalt, is a member of OeKB's non-executive board.
OeKB, Austria's central securities depository and the government's financing agent, is jointly owned by the country's leading commercial banks.
Bank Austria, which now controls Creditanstalt, denied that it had received any secret payments from OeKB or was in any way involved in tax evasion.
"This was a special dividend which was paid to all owners. It was planned and authorised," spokesman Heimo Hackel told Reuters.
Haider made special reference to one page in the documents which showed handwriting, said to be Praschak's, outlining the alleged secret payment. The documents were made available to reporters.
Haider said the papers showed the payment was disguised as fees and provisions on credit lines granted by the banks to OeKB. These credit lines were never drawn upon, he added.
"The question is whether this is a one-off occurrence or whether this kind of thing has happened often," Haider said.
Haider and the opposition Greens, who also received the documents, called for an immediate parliamentary inquiry into the allegations.
In suicide notes left at his Vienna home and office, Praschak also cited political reasons for taking his life.
He claimed his career was threatened by last week's appointment to the OeKB board of former arts and transport minister Rudolf Scholten.

Haider said the papers showed Praschak had felt political pressure to make room for Scholten, who left government after chancellor Franz Vranitzky resigned in January. Finance minister Viktor Klima was named new chancellor.
"The name Klima comes up repeatedly," Haider said. "The chancellor had a hand in this."
Both Klima and Randa denied that they had exerted any political pressure on Praschak or that they had suggested to him to quit his seat on OeKB's board for Scholten.
"There was no political or any similar pressure at all," Klima told Austrian state radio.
Bank Austria said it had not seen Praschak's notes. "That is the interpretation of somebody who died in a very tragic way," Hackel added.
